context: Regulation 16(2): If the client does not co-operate with the credit rating agency so as to enable the credit rating agency to comply with its obligations under regulation 15, the credit rating agency shall carry out the review on the basis of the best available information or in the manner as specified by the Board from time to time. Provided that if owing to such lack of co-operation, a rating has been based on the best available information, the credit rating agency shall disclose to the investors the fact that the rating is so based. (3) A credit rating agency shall not withdraw a rating so long as the obligations under the security rated by it are outstanding, except where the company whose security is rated is wound up or merged or amalgamated with another company.
question: What must a credit rating agency do if a client fails to cooperate during the rating review process under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999? Can a CRA withdraw a rating while the security's obligations are outstanding?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 16(2), if the client does not cooperate with the credit rating agency during the review process, the CRA shall carry out the review on the basis of the best available information or in the manner specified by SEBI from time to time. If a rating has been based on best available information due to such lack of co-operation, the CRA must disclose this fact to investors. Under Regulation 16(3), a CRA shall NOT withdraw a rating so long as the obligations under the rated security are outstanding. The only exceptions permitting withdrawal are: (a) the company whose security is rated is wound up, or (b) merged or amalgamated with another company.

context: Regulation 28E(m)(iv): [Category I ESG rating provider] the applicant shall maintain a minimum liquid net worth of rupees five crores at all times: Provided that at the time of making the application, the applicant shall have a minimum liquid net worth of the higher of, A. rupees ten crores, or B. addition of rupees five crores and the target on cumulative cash losses until breakeven.
question: What are the ongoing and application-time liquid net worth requirements for a Category I ESG rating provider under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
YOUR_ANSWER: Ongoing requirement: A Category I ESG rating provider must maintain a minimum liquid net worth of Rs 5 crore at all times. Application-time requirement: At the time of making the application, the applicant must have a minimum liquid net worth of the HIGHER of: (A) Rs 10 crore, OR (B) Rs 5 crore plus the target on cumulative cash losses until breakeven.

context: Regulation 9(2): For purposes of payment by way of listed shares, the shares sought to be issued or exchanged shall conform to the following: (a) listed and frequently traded; (b) listed for at least two years preceding the date of public announcement; (c) issuer has redressed at least 95% of complaints received from investors in the preceding calendar quarter; (d) issuer has been in material compliance with listing regulations for at least two years immediately preceding the date of public announcement; (e) impact of auditors' qualifications does not exceed 5% of net profit or loss after tax for three immediately preceding financial years; (f) SEBI has not issued directions against the issuer restricting capital market access.
question: What conditions must listed shares offered as non-cash consideration in an open offer satisfy under Regulation 9(2) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 9(2), listed shares offered as non-cash consideration in an open offer must satisfy all of the following conditions: (a) they are listed and frequently traded; (b) they have been listed for at least two years preceding the date of public announcement; (c) the issuer has redressed at least 95% of complaints received from investors in the preceding calendar quarter; (d) the issuer has been in material compliance with listing regulations for at least two years immediately preceding the date of public announcement; (e) the impact of auditors' qualifications does not exceed 5% of net profit or loss after tax for the three immediately preceding financial years; (f) SEBI has not issued directions against the issuer restricting access to the capital market.

context: Regulation 24A(1): A credit rating agency shall not: (a) directly or indirectly, hold 10 per cent or more shareholding and/or voting rights in any other credit rating agency, or (b) have representation on the Board of any other credit rating agency. (2) A shareholder holding 10 per cent or more shares and/or voting rights in a credit rating agency shall not hold 10 per cent or more shares and/or voting rights, directly or indirectly, in any other credit rating agency. Provided that the said restriction shall not apply to holdings by Pension Funds, Insurance Schemes and Mutual Fund Schemes.
question: What shareholding restrictions apply between credit rating agencies under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999? Are there any exemptions?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 24A(1): (a) No CRA shall directly or indirectly hold 10% or more shareholding and/or voting rights in any other CRA, and (b) no CRA shall have representation on the Board of any other CRA. Under Regulation 24A(2): A shareholder holding 10% or more shares and/or voting rights in a CRA shall not hold 10% or more shares and/or voting rights, directly or indirectly, in any other CRA. Exemption: The restriction in sub-regulation (2) does not apply to holdings by Pension Funds, Insurance Schemes, and Mutual Fund Schemes.

context: Regulation 26(2): During the offer period, unless the approval of shareholders of the target company by way of a special resolution by postal ballot is obtained, the board of directors of either the target company or any of its subsidiaries shall not: (a) alienate any material assets outside ordinary course of business; (b) effect any material borrowings outside ordinary course of business; (c) issue or allot any authorised but unissued securities entitling voting rights; (d) implement any buy-back or effect capital structure changes; (e) enter into, amend or terminate material contracts outside ordinary course; (f) accelerate any contingent vesting of rights including ESOPs.
question: Under Regulation 26(2) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011, what actions is the target company's board of directors prohibited from taking during the offer period without shareholder approval by postal ballot?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 26(2), unless shareholder approval is obtained by special resolution through postal ballot, the board of directors of the target company (or any of its subsidiaries) shall not during the offer period: (a) alienate any material assets outside the ordinary course of business; (b) effect any material borrowings outside the ordinary course of business; (c) issue or allot any authorised but unissued securities entitling voting rights; (d) implement any buy-back or effect capital structure changes; (e) enter into, amend or terminate material contracts outside the ordinary course of business; (f) accelerate any contingent vesting of rights, including ESOPs.

context: Regulation 16(1)(c): Category I Alternative Investment Funds shall not borrow funds directly or indirectly or engage in any leverage for the purpose of making investments or otherwise, except for borrowing funds to meet temporary funding requirements and day-to-day operational requirements for not more than thirty days, on not more than four occasions in a year and not more than ten percent of the investable funds.
question: Under what conditions may a Category I Alternative Investment Fund borrow funds under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012? What are the specific restrictions on such borrowing?
YOUR_ANSWER: A Category I AIF may borrow funds only to meet temporary funding requirements and day-to-day operational requirements. Three specific restrictions apply cumulatively to such borrowing: (1) Duration: not more than thirty days per borrowing instance; (2) Frequency: not more than four occasions in a year; (3) Quantum: not more than ten percent of the investable funds. Borrowing for any purpose other than temporary funding and operational requirements is not permitted.

context: Regulation 27(1): No credit rating agency shall rate a security issued by an entity which is — (a) a borrower of its promoter; or (b) a subsidiary of its promoter; or (c) an associate of its promoter, if there are common Chairman, Directors between credit rating agency and these entities, or common employees, or common Chairman, Directors, Employees on the rating committee. (2) No credit rating agency shall rate a security issued by its associate or subsidiary, if the credit rating agency or its rating committee has a Chairman, director or employee who is also a Chairman, director or employee of any such entity.
question: What conflict-of-interest restrictions apply to the rating of securities of promoter-connected entities under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 27(1): No CRA shall rate a security issued by an entity that is (a) a borrower of its promoter, (b) a subsidiary of its promoter, or (c) an associate of its promoter, IF there are common Chairman or Directors between the CRA and those entities, or common employees, or common Chairman, Directors, or Employees on the rating committee. Under Regulation 27(2): No CRA shall rate a security issued by its own associate or subsidiary if the CRA or its rating committee has a Chairman, director or employee who is also a Chairman, director or employee of any such associate or subsidiary entity.

context: Regulation 15(7): An investment advisor shall not enter into transactions on its own account which is contrary to its advice given to clients for a period of fifteen days from the day of such advice. Provided that during the period of such fifteen days, if the investment adviser is of the opinion that the situation has changed, then it may enter into such a transaction on its own account after giving such revised assessment to the client at least 24 hours in advance of entering into such transaction.
question: Under SEBI IA Regulations, 2013, if an investment adviser advised clients to buy a stock on a certain date but subsequently believes the situation has changed within 10 days, can the adviser immediately sell the same stock from its own account?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, the adviser cannot immediately sell. Under Regulation 15(7), the investment adviser is prohibited from entering into transactions contrary to the advice given to clients for a period of fifteen days from the day of such advice. Since only 10 days have elapsed, the adviser is still within the 15-day prohibition window. However, the proviso permits an exception: if the adviser is of the opinion that the situation has changed within those 15 days, it may enter into the contrary own-account transaction ONLY after giving a revised assessment to the client at least 24 hours in advance of entering into such transaction. Accordingly, the adviser must first issue the revised assessment to clients, then wait at least 24 hours before executing the sale from its own account.

context: Regulation 22A: (1) Investment adviser may provide implementation services to the advisory clients in securities market: Provided that investment advisers shall ensure that no consideration including any commission or referral fees, whether embedded or indirect or otherwise, by whatever name called is received; directly or indirectly, at investment adviser's group or family level for the said service. (2) Investment adviser shall provide implementation services to its advisory clients only through direct schemes/products in the securities market. (3) Investment adviser or group or family of investment adviser shall not charge any implementation fees from the client. (4) The client shall not be under any obligation to avail implementation services offered by the investment adviser.
question: Under SEBI IA Regulations, 2013, what are the four key conditions governing an investment adviser's provision of implementation services to advisory clients?
YOUR_ANSWER: The four key conditions governing an investment adviser's provision of implementation services under Regulation 22A are: (1) No consideration (including any commission or referral fees, whether embedded, indirect, or otherwise) shall be received directly or indirectly at the investment adviser's group or family level for the said service; (2) Implementation services shall be provided to advisory clients only through direct schemes/products in the securities market; (3) Neither the investment adviser nor its group or family shall charge any implementation fees from the client; (4) The client shall not be under any obligation to avail the implementation services offered by the investment adviser.

context: Regulation 10(3): An increase in voting rights in a target company of any shareholder beyond the limit attracting an obligation to make an open offer under sub-regulation (1) of regulation 3, pursuant to buy-back of shares by the target company shall be exempt from the obligation to make an open offer provided such shareholder reduces his shareholding such that his voting rights fall to below the threshold referred to in sub-regulation (1) of regulation 3 within ninety days from the date of the closure of the said buy-back offer.
question: Under Regulation 10(3), what must a shareholder do to claim exemption from making an open offer when their voting rights exceed the threshold solely because of a buy-back by the target company?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 10(3), to claim exemption from the open offer obligation when voting rights exceed the threshold solely due to a buy-back by the target company, the shareholder must reduce its shareholding such that its voting rights fall BELOW the threshold referred to in sub-regulation (1) of Regulation 3 WITHIN NINETY DAYS from the date of the closure of the said buy-back offer. Failure to reduce shareholding within this 90-day window would mean the exemption is not available.

context: Regulation 13(e): individuals registered as investment advisers whose number of clients exceed three hundred at any point of time or the fee collected during the financial year exceeds three crore rupees, whichever is earlier shall — (i) immediately intimate the Administration and Supervisory Body and initiate the process of transition from individual to non-individual investment adviser; and (ii) apply for grant of in-principle approval for registration as non-individual investment adviser within 3 months from the date on which the threshold is reached.
question: Under SEBI IA Regulations, 2013, what dual threshold triggers the mandatory transition of an individual investment adviser to non-individual status, and what must the IA do upon breaching the threshold?
YOUR_ANSWER: The dual threshold that triggers mandatory transition is: (i) the number of clients exceeds 300 at any point of time, OR (ii) the fee collected during the financial year exceeds Rs 3 crore — whichever occurs earlier. Upon breaching either threshold, the individual IA must: (i) immediately intimate the Administration and Supervisory Body and initiate the process of transition from individual to non-individual investment adviser; and (ii) apply for grant of in-principle approval for registration as a non-individual investment adviser within 3 months from the date on which the threshold is reached.

context: Seventh Schedule — Restrictions on Investments. 1. A mutual fund scheme shall not invest more than 10% of its NAV in debt instruments comprising money market instruments and non-money market instruments issued by a single issuer which are rated not below investment grade by a credit rating agency authorised to carry out such activity under the Act. Such investment limit may be extended to 12% of the NAV of the scheme with the prior approval of the Board of Trustees and Board of Directors of the asset management company: Provided that such limit shall not be applicable for investments in Government Securities, treasury bills and triparty repo on Government securities or treasury bills.
question: Under the Seventh Schedule of SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, what is the standard investment limit for debt instruments issued by a single issuer, and under what approval can it be extended to 12% of NAV?
YOUR_ANSWER: The standard investment limit is 10% of the scheme's NAV in debt instruments (comprising both money market instruments and non-money market instruments) issued by a single issuer, provided such instruments are rated not below investment grade by an authorised credit rating agency. This limit may be extended to 12% of NAV with the prior approval of both the Board of Trustees AND the Board of Directors of the asset management company. The limit does not apply to investments in Government Securities, treasury bills, and triparty repo on Government securities or treasury bills.

context: Payment of annual service fee. 12. A mutual fund shall pay before the 15th April each year a service fee as specified in the Second Schedule for every financial year from the year following the year of registration: Provided that the Board may, on being satisfied with the reasons for the delay permit the mutual fund to pay the service fee at any time before the expiry of two months from the commencement of the financial year to which such fee relates.
question: By what date must a mutual fund pay its annual service fee, and what is the maximum grace period SEBI may allow for a delayed payment?
YOUR_ANSWER: A mutual fund must pay its annual service fee before the 15th April of each year (for the financial year following the year of registration). SEBI may, if satisfied with the reasons for delay, permit the mutual fund to pay the fee at any time before the expiry of two months from the commencement of the financial year to which such fee relates. Since the financial year commences on April 1, this grace period extends to the end of May (i.e., by May 31).

context: Seventh Schedule — Restrictions on Investments. 9. No mutual fund [scheme] shall make any investment in— (a) any unlisted security of an associate or group company of the sponsor; or (b) any security issued by way of private placement by an associate or group company of the sponsor; or (c) the listed securities of group companies of the sponsor which is in excess of 25 per cent of the net assets.
question: What two categories of securities of associate or group companies of the sponsor are absolutely prohibited for mutual fund investment under the Seventh Schedule?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under paragraph 9 of the Seventh Schedule, two categories of securities are absolutely prohibited for mutual fund scheme investment: (a) any unlisted security of an associate or group company of the sponsor; and (b) any security issued by way of private placement by an associate or group company of the sponsor. (Note: Listed securities of group companies of the sponsor are not absolutely prohibited but are capped at 25% of net assets under clause (c).)

context: Seventh Schedule — Restrictions on Investments. 13. A mutual fund scheme shall not invest — i. more than 10% of its NAV in the units of InvIT; and ii. more than 5% of its NAV in the units of InvIT issued by a single issuer. Provided that the limits mentioned in sub-clauses (i) and (ii) above shall not be applicable for investments in case of index fund or sector or industry specific scheme pertaining to REIT and InvIT.
question: What are the NAV-based investment limits for a mutual fund scheme in InvIT units — both the overall cap and the cap for units issued by a single InvIT issuer?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under paragraph 13 of the Seventh Schedule, a mutual fund scheme may not invest: (i) more than 10% of its NAV in the units of InvIT in aggregate (overall cap); and (ii) more than 5% of its NAV in the units of InvIT issued by any single InvIT issuer (per-issuer cap). Exception: Both limits are not applicable for investments by index funds or sector/industry specific schemes pertaining to REIT and InvIT.

context: Seventh Schedule — Restrictions on Investments. 4. A scheme may invest in another scheme under the same asset management company or any other mutual fund without charging any fees, provided that aggregate inter-scheme investment made by all schemes under the same management or in schemes under the management of any other asset management company shall not exceed 5% of the net asset value of the mutual fund: Provided that this clause shall not apply to any fund of funds scheme.
question: What is the maximum aggregate inter-scheme investment that all schemes under one AMC's management may collectively make in other mutual funds?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under paragraph 4 of the Seventh Schedule, the aggregate inter-scheme investment made by all schemes under the same AMC management (or in schemes under the management of any other asset management company) shall not exceed 5% of the net asset value of the mutual fund. Such inter-scheme investments must be made without charging any fees. Exception: This restriction does not apply to any fund of funds scheme.

context: "institutional investor" means â€” (i) a qualified institutional buyer; or (ii) a family trust or an intermediary registered with the Board, having a net worth of more than five hundred crore rupees, as per the latest audited financial statements.
question: Under SEBI (InvIT) Regulations 2014 (as currently in force), what minimum net worth must a family trust or a Board-registered intermediary have to qualify as an institutional investor?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under SEBI (InvIT) Regulations 2014, a family trust or an intermediary registered with the Board must have a net worth of MORE THAN Rs 500 crore, as per the latest audited financial statements, to qualify as an 'institutional investor'. (The other category of institutional investor under this definition is a qualified institutional buyer, for which no minimum net worth is separately specified here.)

context: Regulation 13(1): Category I Alternative Investment Fund and Category II Alternative Investment Fund shall be close ended and the tenure of fund or scheme shall be determined at the time of application subject to sub-regulation (2) of this regulation. (2) Category I and II Alternative Investment Fund or schemes launched by such funds shall have a minimum tenure of three years. (3) Schemes of Category III Alternative Investment Fund may be open ended or close ended.
question: What are the structural and tenure requirements applicable to Category I and II Alternative Investment Funds, and how do they differ from Category III AIFs?
YOUR_ANSWER: Category I and II AIFs must be CLOSE ENDED; the tenure of the fund or scheme is determined at the time of application, subject to sub-regulation (2). Both Category I and II AIFs (or schemes launched by such funds) must have a MINIMUM TENURE OF THREE YEARS. Category III AIF schemes may be EITHER OPEN ENDED OR CLOSE ENDED — there is no structural restriction or minimum tenure requirement specified for Category III.

context: Investment, borrowing, restriction, etc. 44. (2) The mutual fund shall not borrow except to meet temporary liquidity needs of the mutual funds for the purpose of repurchase, redemption of units or payment of interest or dividend to the unitholders: Provided that the mutual fund shall not borrow more than 20 per cent of the net asset of the scheme and the duration of such a borrowing shall not exceed a period of six months.
question: For what purpose may a mutual fund borrow under SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, and what are the two quantitative limits on such borrowing?
YOUR_ANSWER: A mutual fund may borrow only to meet TEMPORARY LIQUIDITY NEEDS for the purpose of repurchase, redemption of units, or payment of interest or dividend to unitholders. Borrowing for any other purpose is not permitted. The two quantitative limits are: (1) Quantum limit: the mutual fund shall not borrow more than 20% of the net asset of the scheme; and (2) Duration limit: the duration of such borrowing shall not exceed a period of six months.

context: The trustee shall review the transactions carried out between the investment manager and its associates and where the investment manager has advised that there may be a conflict of interest, shall obtain confirmation from a practising chartered accountant or valuer, as applicable, that such transaction is on arm's length basis.
question: Under SEBI (InvIT) Regulations 2014, when a conflict of interest is flagged in a transaction between the investment manager and its associates, from whom must the trustee obtain confirmation that the transaction is at arm's length?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under SEBI (InvIT) Regulations 2014, when the investment manager has advised that there may be a conflict of interest in a transaction between the investment manager and its associates, the trustee must review the transaction and obtain confirmation from a PRACTISING CHARTERED ACCOUNTANT OR VALUER, as applicable, that such transaction is on an arm's length basis.

context: Regulation 22(2): Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-regulation (1), subject to the acquirer depositing in the escrow account cash of an amount equal to the entire consideration payable under the open offer assuming full acceptance of the open offer, the parties to such agreement may after the expiry of twenty-one working days from the date of detailed public statement, act upon the agreement and the acquirer may complete the acquisition.
question: Under what condition and after what period may an acquirer complete the underlying acquisition before the expiry of the offer period under Regulation 22(2)?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 22(2), the acquirer may complete the underlying acquisition (and parties to the agreement may act upon it) after the expiry of TWENTY-ONE WORKING DAYS from the date of the detailed public statement, PROVIDED THAT the acquirer has deposited in the escrow account CASH of an amount equal to the ENTIRE CONSIDERATION payable under the open offer assuming full acceptance of the open offer. This is an exception to the general rule in sub-regulation (1) that prohibits acting on the agreement during the offer period.

context: Regulation 10(d): the Manager or Sponsor shall have a continuing interest in the Alternative Investment Fund of not less than two and half percent of the corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is lower, in the form of investment in the Alternative Investment Fund and such interest shall not be through the waiver of management fees: Provided that for Category III Alternative Investment Fund, the continuing interest shall be not less than five percent of the corpus or ten crore rupees, whichever is lower.
question: What continuing interest is the Manager or Sponsor of an Alternative Investment Fund required to maintain under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012? Does the requirement differ between Category I/II and Category III funds?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 10(d), the Manager or Sponsor must maintain a continuing interest in the AIF in the form of actual investment in the AIF (not through waiver of management fees). For Category I and II AIFs: the continuing interest must be not less than 2.5% of the corpus OR Rs 5 crore, WHICHEVER IS LOWER. For Category III AIF: the continuing interest must be not less than 5% of the corpus OR Rs 10 crore, WHICHEVER IS LOWER. Yes, the requirement differs — Category III requires a higher absolute and proportionate continuing interest than Category I/II.

context: Regulation 16(2)(a): at least seventy-five percent of the investable funds shall be invested in unlisted equity shares or equity linked instruments of a venture capital undertaking or in companies listed or proposed to be listed on a SME exchange or SME segment of an exchange: Provided that the investment conditions specified in clause (a) shall be achieved by the fund by the end of its life cycle.
question: What minimum percentage of investable funds must a venture capital fund (which is a sub-category of Category I AIF) invest in qualifying instruments under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 16(2)(a), a venture capital fund (Category I AIF sub-category) must invest at least 75% of its investable funds in: unlisted equity shares or equity linked instruments of a venture capital undertaking, OR in companies listed or proposed to be listed on a SME exchange or SME segment of an exchange. This 75% investment condition must be achieved by the fund by the end of its life cycle.

context: Regulation 10(c): the Alternative Investment Fund shall not accept from an investor, an investment of value less than one crore rupees: Provided that in case of investors who are employees or directors of the Alternative Investment Fund or employees or directors of the Manager, the minimum value of investment shall be twenty five lakh rupees: Provided further that this clause shall not apply to an accredited investor.
question: What is the minimum investment that an investor must make in an Alternative Investment Fund scheme under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012? Are there any exceptions to this minimum?
YOUR_ANSWER: The minimum investment per investor in an AIF scheme is Rs 1 CRORE. Exception 1 (reduced minimum): For investors who are employees or directors of the AIF, or employees or directors of the Manager, the minimum investment is Rs 25 LAKH. Exception 2 (full exemption): An ACCREDITED INVESTOR is fully exempt from this minimum investment requirement — the minimum threshold does not apply.

context: Regulation 6A: Notwithstanding anything contained in these regulations, no person who is a wilful defaulter shall make a public announcement of an open offer for acquiring shares or enter into any transaction that would attract the obligation to make a public announcement of an open offer for acquiring shares under these regulations. Provided that this regulation shall not prohibit the wilful defaulter from making a competing offer upon any other person making an open offer for acquiring shares of the target company.
question: What does Regulation 6A of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011 prohibit, and what exception does it carve out for wilful defaulters?
YOUR_ANSWER: Regulation 6A prohibits any person who is a WILFUL DEFAULTER from: (i) making a public announcement of an open offer for acquiring shares, or (ii) entering into any transaction that would attract the obligation to make such a public announcement of an open offer. Exception carved out: The regulation does not prohibit a wilful defaulter from making a COMPETING OFFER upon any OTHER person making an open offer for acquiring shares of the target company. In that specific scenario, the wilful defaulter may participate as a competing bidder.

context: No company shall directly or indirectly purchase its own shares or other specified securities: (a) through any subsidiary company including its own subsidiary companies; (b) through any investment company or group of investment companies; or (c) if a default is made by the company in the repayment of deposits...Provided that the buy-back is not prohibited, if the default is remedied and a period of three years has lapsed after such default ceased to subsist.
question: A company defaulted on repayment of a term loan. The default was remedied. After how long can the company conduct a buy-back?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under the proviso to the relevant provision, a company that has defaulted on repayment may conduct a buy-back only if TWO CONDITIONS are jointly satisfied: (1) the default has been remedied, AND (2) a period of THREE YEARS has lapsed after such default ceased to subsist. Therefore, the company must wait three years from the date the default ceased to subsist before it can conduct a buy-back.

context: Annex I: Illustration 3: Computation of maximum eligible dividend for FY 20X1-X2. Net profit (PAT) for FY 20X1-X2 (A): Rs1,500 crore. Net NPAs as on March 31, 20X2 (B): Rs300 crore. Adjusted PAT, i.e., (C) = (A) - 50% of (B): Rs1,350 crore. Tier 1 capital ratio as on March 31, 20X1 (D): 24.36% (falls in Bucket B10). 75% of PAT (E): Rs1,125 crore. Maximum payable as per Table (100% of 1,350) (F): Rs1,350 crore. Maximum Eligible Dividend (G = Lower of E or F): Rs1,125 crore. Interim dividend paid for FY 20X1-20X2 (H): Rs500 crore. As the bank has already paid interim dividend of Rs500 crore, the final dividend shall not be more than (G) - (H).
question: In Illustration 3, a bank has PAT of Rs1,500 crore, Net NPA of Rs300 crore, Tier 1 ratio of 24.36%, and has already paid interim dividend of Rs500 crore. What is the maximum final dividend it may pay?
YOUR_ANSWER: From Illustration 3: Adjusted PAT (C) = Rs 1,500 crore minus 50% of Rs 300 crore = Rs 1,350 crore. 75% of PAT (E) = Rs 1,125 crore. Maximum payable per table at Bucket B10 (100% of Adjusted PAT) (F) = Rs 1,350 crore. Maximum Eligible Dividend (G) = Lower of E or F = Rs 1,125 crore. Less interim dividend already paid (H) = Rs 500 crore. Maximum FINAL dividend = G minus H = Rs 1,125 crore minus Rs 500 crore = Rs 625 crore.

context: Regulation 15(7): An investment advisor shall not enter into transactions on its own account which is contrary to its advice given to clients for a period of fifteen days from the day of such advice. Provided that during the period of such fifteen days, if the investment adviser is of the opinion that the situation has changed, then it may enter into such a transaction on its own account after giving such revised assessment to the client at least 24 hours in advance of entering into such transaction.
question: An investment adviser issues a buy recommendation on Stock A to clients on January 10. On January 22, the adviser believes the situation has changed and wants to sell Stock A from its own account. Is January 22 within the 15-day prohibition window? If the adviser gives clients a revised assessment on January 22 at 3:00 PM, what is the earliest date and time at which the adviser can enter the contrary own-account sell transaction?
YOUR_ANSWER: The 15-day prohibition runs from January 10 (Day 1) through January 24 (Day 15). January 22 is Day 13, which is within the 15-day prohibition window. Under the proviso to Regulation 15(7), since the adviser believes the situation has changed within the 15-day window, the adviser must give a revised assessment to the client at least 24 hours BEFORE entering the contrary own-account transaction. If the revised assessment is given on January 22 at 3:00 PM, then 24 hours later = January 23 at 3:00 PM. The earliest date and time the adviser can enter the contrary sell transaction is January 23 at 3:00 PM.

context: Regulation 10(c): the Alternative Investment Fund shall not accept from an investor, an investment of value less than one crore rupees: Provided that in case of investors who are employees or directors of the Alternative Investment Fund or employees or directors of the Manager, the minimum value of investment shall be twenty five lakh rupees.
question: A Category II AIF has 4 investors: an external institutional investor, a director of the Manager, an employee of the AIF, and an accredited investor. Their proposed investments are Rs 75 lakh, Rs 20 lakh, Rs 30 lakh, and Rs 50 lakh respectively. Which investments, if any, fail to meet the minimum investment requirements under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012?
YOUR_ANSWER: Applicable minimum investment thresholds under Regulation 10(c): (i) General investors: Rs 1 crore; (ii) Employees/directors of the AIF or Manager: Rs 25 lakh; (iii) Accredited investors: exempt (no minimum). Assessment of proposed investments: (a) External institutional investor: proposed Rs 75 lakh vs minimum Rs 1 crore — FAILS (shortfall of Rs 25 lakh). (b) Director of the Manager: proposed Rs 20 lakh vs minimum Rs 25 lakh — FAILS (shortfall of Rs 5 lakh). (c) Employee of the AIF: proposed Rs 30 lakh vs minimum Rs 25 lakh — PASSES. (d) Accredited investor: proposed Rs 50 lakh, fully exempt from minimum — PASSES. Conclusion: The external institutional investor and the director of the Manager fail to meet the minimum investment requirements.

context: Annex I: Illustration 1: Computation of maximum permissible dividend for FY 20X1-X2. Net profit (PAT) for FY 20X1-X2 (A): Rs17,000 crore. Net NPAs as on March 31, 20X2 (B): Rs6,500 crore. context: Regulation 15(7): An investment advisor shall not enter into transactions on its own account which is contrary to its advice given to clients for a period of fifteen days from the day of such advice. Provided that during the period of such fifteen days, if the investment adviser is of the opinion that the situation has changed, then it may enter into such a transaction on its own account after giving such revised assessment to the client at least 24 hours in advance of entering into such transaction.
question: An investment adviser gave clients a sell recommendation on Bond X on April 1. On April 14, the adviser issues a revised assessment to clients. On April 16, the adviser wants to buy Bond X for its own account (contrary to the original sell recommendation). Is the April 16 transaction permissible?
YOUR_ANSWER: The 15-day prohibition runs from April 1 (Day 1) through April 15 (Day 15). The revised assessment was issued on April 14 (Day 14), which is within the 15-day window — satisfying the proviso's requirement. Under the proviso, the adviser may enter the contrary transaction at least 24 hours after giving the revised assessment to clients. 24 hours after April 14 = April 15. April 16 is both after the 24-hour notice period AND after the 15-day prohibition window (which ends on April 15). YES, the April 16 transaction is permissible. The adviser has satisfied both conditions: revised assessment given within the 15-day window, and at least 24 hours have elapsed before the transaction.

context: Regulation 8(10): Where the acquirer acquires shares during the period of twenty-six weeks after the tendering period at a price higher than the offer price, the acquirer shall pay the difference between the highest acquisition price and the offer price to all shareholders whose shares were accepted in the open offer, within sixty days from the date of such acquisition.
question: An open offer at Rs 100 per share completed payment to shareholders on March 15, 2024. The acquirer then purchases shares in the open market at Rs 130 per share on August 20, 2024. Does Regulation 8(10) apply, and if so, by when must the difference be paid to shareholders who tendered in the open offer?
YOUR_ANSWER: YES, Regulation 8(10) applies. The open offer tendering period completed with payment on March 15, 2024. 26 weeks from March 15, 2024 = approximately September 14, 2024. The acquirer's open-market purchase at Rs 130 per share occurred on August 20, 2024, which falls within the 26-week window after the tendering period. Since the acquisition price (Rs 130) exceeds the offer price (Rs 100), the acquirer must pay the difference of Rs 30 per share to all shareholders whose shares were accepted in the open offer. Deadline: within 60 days from August 20, 2024 = by October 19, 2024.

question: Institution X holds 12% of the shares of CRA-1. It proposes to acquire a 9% stake in CRA-2. Would this acquisition violate Regulation 24A(2) of the SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
YOUR_ANSWER: Regulation 24A(2) prohibits a shareholder holding 10% or more in one CRA from also holding 10% or more in any other CRA. Institution X holds 12% in CRA-1 (above the 10% threshold — the restriction is triggered). The proposed acquisition is a 9% stake in CRA-2, which is BELOW the 10% threshold in CRA-2. Since the restriction under Regulation 24A(2) is triggered only when the shareholder holds 10% or more in BOTH CRAs, a 9% holding in CRA-2 does not breach the restriction. Conclusion: The proposed acquisition would NOT violate Regulation 24A(2).

question: An AIF Manager is planning to launch three schemes: Scheme A (private equity fund), Scheme B (social impact fund), and Scheme C (infrastructure fund). What is the minimum total corpus that must be raised across all three schemes to comply with SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 10(b): the minimum corpus per scheme is Rs 20 crore, except for a social impact fund scheme, which requires a minimum of Rs 5 crore. Minimum corpus calculation: Scheme A (private equity fund): Rs 20 crore. Scheme B (social impact fund): Rs 5 crore. Scheme C (infrastructure fund): Rs 20 crore. Total minimum corpus = Rs 20 + Rs 5 + Rs 20 = Rs 45 crore.

context: Regulation 13(e): individuals registered as investment advisers whose number of clients exceed three hundred at any point of time or the fee collected during the financial year exceeds three crore rupees, whichever is earlier shall immediately initiate the process of transition from individual to non-individual investment adviser.
question: An individual investment adviser collected fees of Rs 2.65 crore in the first eight months of the financial year. In the ninth month they collected Rs 0.22 crore and in the tenth month Rs 0.18 crore. At the end of which month is the fee-based transition threshold breached, and what is the total fee at that point?
YOUR_ANSWER: The fee-based transition threshold is reached when cumulative fees collected during the financial year exceed Rs 3 crore. Running total: After 8 months = Rs 2.65 crore. After Month 9 (Rs 0.22 crore added): cumulative total = Rs 2.87 crore (below threshold). After Month 10 (Rs 0.18 crore added): cumulative total = Rs 3.05 crore (exceeds Rs 3 crore). The fee-based threshold of Rs 3 crore is breached at the end of Month 10, with total fees of Rs 3.05 crore.

question: Under SEBI (Issue and Listing of Municipal Debt Securities) Regulations 2015, if a roll-over notice is dispatched to holders on 5 May 2025, what is the earliest date on which the roll-over can take effect (assuming all holders consent)?
YOUR_ANSWER: The regulation requires the issuer to give twenty-one days' notice of the proposed roll-over to holders of municipal debt securities. Notice dispatched on 5 May 2025. Counting 21 days from May 5: the 21-day notice period expires on May 25, 2025 (Day 21). The roll-over can take effect at the earliest on May 26, 2025 (the day after the notice period has fully elapsed), assuming all holders provide consent within the notice period.

context: Regulation 15(1)(c): Category I and II of Alternative Investment Funds shall invest not more than twenty five per cent of the investable funds in an Investee Company directly or through investment in the units of other Alternative Investment Funds.
question: A Category II AIF has investable funds of Rs 400 crore. The Manager wants to invest Rs 120 crore in Company X. Is this investment permissible? What is the maximum amount that can be invested in Company X?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 15(1)(c), Category I and II AIFs shall not invest more than 25% of investable funds in a single investee company. Maximum permissible investment = 25% of Rs 400 crore = Rs 100 crore. Proposed investment of Rs 120 crore exceeds this limit (Rs 120 crore > Rs 100 crore). Conclusion: The proposed investment of Rs 120 crore in Company X is NOT permissible. The maximum permissible amount that can be invested in Company X is Rs 100 crore.

Regulation 9(f) (pre-Second Amendment 2018): a credit rating agency shall not carry out any activity other than the rating of securities offered by way of public or rights issue. Provided that nothing in these regulations shall prohibit a credit rating agency from engaging in any other activity in so far as it may be required by a financial sector regulator.

question: Do the original and 2018-amended versions of Regulation 9(f) define the same permissible scope of rating activities for a credit rating agency?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, the original and 2018-amended versions of Regulation 9(f) do NOT define the same permissible scope of rating activities. The original version restricted CRA activities to 'rating of securities offered by way of public or rights issue' — i.e., only primary market issuances. The 2018-amended version (w.e.f. 11-09-2018) expanded this to 'rating of securities that are listed or proposed to be listed on a stock exchange recognized by the Board', which covers both primary and secondary market listed securities, a materially broader scope. Additionally, the original proviso permitted 'any other activity required by a financial sector regulator' broadly, while the 2018 version restricts other activities to those specifically prescribed or permitted by the Board. The two versions therefore impose meaningfully different scope restrictions on CRA rating activities.

context:
Passage A:
A mutual fund scheme shall not invest more than 10% of its NAV in unrated debt instruments issued by a single issuer and the total investment in such instruments shall not exceed 25% of the NAV of the scheme. All such investments shall be made with the prior approval of the Board of Trustees and the Board of asset management company.

Passage B:
A mutual fund scheme shall not invest in unlisted debt instruments including commercial papers, except Government Securities and other money market instruments: Provided that Mutual Fund Schemes may invest in unlisted non-convertible debentures up to a maximum of 10% of the debt portfolio of the scheme subject to such conditions as may be specified by the Board from time to time.
question: Do Passage A and Passage B impose the same restriction on investments in unrated or unlisted debt instruments?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, Passage A and Passage B do NOT impose the same restriction — they address fundamentally different attributes of debt instruments. Passage A restricts investments in UNRATED debt instruments: capped at 10% of NAV per single issuer and 25% of NAV in aggregate, with prior approval of the Board of Trustees and Board of AMC. Passage B restricts investments in UNLISTED debt instruments: generally prohibited (except Government Securities and money market instruments), with a limited carve-out of up to 10% of the DEBT PORTFOLIO (not NAV) for unlisted NCDs, subject to Board-specified conditions. The restrictions operate along different dimensions (rating status vs. listing status), use different denominators (NAV vs. debt portfolio), and carry different approval mechanisms. They are complementary but not the same restriction.

context:
Passage A:
Regulation 3(2): No acquirer who together with persons acting in concert holds 25% or more but less than the maximum permissible non-public shareholding shall acquire within any financial year additional shares or voting rights entitling them to exercise more than five per cent of the voting rights, unless an open offer is made.

Passage B:
Regulation 3(2) proviso (inserted by Amendment Regulations, 2020, w.e.f. 16-06-2020): Provided that the acquisition beyond five per cent but upto ten per cent of the voting rights in the target company shall be permitted for the financial year 2020-21 only in respect of acquisition by a promoter pursuant to preferential issue of equity shares by the target company.
question: Do the main provision and the 2020 proviso of Regulation 3(2) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011 contradict each other about the annual creep acquisition limit?
YOUR_ANSWER: There is NO contradiction between the main provision and the 2020 proviso of Regulation 3(2). The main provision sets the standard annual creep acquisition limit at 5% of voting rights for acquirers holding 25% or more. The 2020 proviso creates a narrow, one-time exception applicable ONLY for FY 2020-21, allowing acquisition beyond 5% and up to 10% of voting rights, but only in the specific case of a promoter acquiring shares pursuant to a preferential issue by the target company. A proviso supplements the main provision by carving out a defined exception; it does not contradict the general rule. Outside the specific conditions of the proviso (i.e., any year other than 2020-21, or any acquirer other than a promoter in a preferential issue), the 5% annual cap continues to apply in full.

context:

Passage B:
An asset management company shall not through any broker associated with the sponsor, purchase or sell securities, which is average of 5 per cent or more of the aggregate purchases and sale of securities made by the mutual fund in all its schemes: Provided further that the aforesaid limit of 5 per cent shall apply for a block of any three months.
question: Do Passage A and Passage B impose the same percentage limit on transactions through sponsor-associated brokers, and is the limit measured over the same time period?
YOUR_ANSWER: Both passages use a 5% threshold, so the percentage limit is the same. However, the two provisions are NOT identical — they measure the 5% against different bases over different time periods. Passage A measures 5% against the DAILY GROSS BUSINESS of the mutual fund (a daily measurement). Passage B measures 5% against the AGGREGATE PURCHASES AND SALES of securities made by the mutual fund in all its schemes over a BLOCK OF THREE MONTHS (a rolling quarterly measurement). The percentage figure is the same (5%) but the benchmark and the time period over which compliance is assessed differ materially — daily gross business vs. three-month aggregate — making the effective restriction different.

context:
Passage A:
No sponsor of a mutual fund, its associate or group company including the asset management company of the fund, through the schemes of the mutual fund or otherwise, individually or collectively, directly or indirectly, have 10% or more of the share-holding or voting rights in the asset management company or the trustee company of any other mutual fund.

Passage B:
Any shareholder holding 10% or more of the share-holding or voting rights in the asset management company or the trustee company of a mutual fund, shall not have, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the share-holding or voting rights in the asset management company or the trustee company of any other mutual fund.
question: Do Passage A and Passage B apply the same shareholding threshold for cross-ownership restrictions in mutual funds?
YOUR_ANSWER: Both passages use a 10% shareholding/voting rights threshold, so the threshold is numerically identical. However, the two passages are NOT the same in scope — they apply to different classes of entities. Passage A applies the 10% cross-ownership restriction specifically to a SPONSOR, its ASSOCIATES, and GROUP COMPANIES (including the AMC) of a mutual fund. Passage B applies the 10% restriction to ANY SHAREHOLDER holding 10% or more in the AMC or trustee company of a mutual fund. Passage B is therefore broader in coverage (any shareholder, not just sponsor and its related parties), while Passage A captures the sponsor-group specifically. The two provisions are complementary — applying the same threshold to different categories of persons.

Passage B:
Regulation 7(1)(a) (as substituted w.e.f. 25-11-2025): A graduate degree or any equivalent educational qualification from a university or institution recognized by the Central Government or any State Government or a recognised foreign university or institution or association or CFA Charter from the CFA Institute, and relevant certification from NISM or from any other organization or institution accredited by NISM.
question: Do the pre-2025 and post-2025 versions of Regulation 7(1)(a) impose the same educational qualification requirement on individual investment advisers?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, the pre-2025 and post-2025 versions impose materially different educational qualification requirements. The pre-2025 version (Passage A) offers multiple alternative pathways: a professional qualification OR graduate/postgraduate degree in a specified list of disciplines (finance, accountancy, business management, commerce, economics, capital market, banking, insurance, actuarial science, or other financial services) from a recognised university, OR completion of NISM's Post Graduate Program in Securities Market (Investment Advisory) of minimum one year duration, OR a CFA Charter from the CFA Institute. Any one of these alternatives sufficed. The post-2025 version (Passage B) requires: (1) a graduate degree or equivalent from a recognised university/institution OR a CFA Charter from CFA Institute, AND (2) a relevant NISM certification (from NISM or an NISM-accredited body). The post-2025 version adds a mandatory NISM certification component (which was absent as a standalone requirement pre-2025), collapses the lengthy list of acceptable disciplines into a general graduate degree requirement, and removes the NISM PGP pathway.

context:
Passage A:
Regulation 23(1): An open offer for acquiring shares once made shall not be withdrawn except: (a) statutory approvals having been finally refused; (b) the acquirer, being a natural person, has died; (c) any condition in the underlying agreement is not met for reasons outside the acquirer's reasonable control; or (d) such circumstances as in the opinion of the Board merit withdrawal.

Passage B:
Regulation 6A: No person who is a wilful defaulter shall make a public announcement of an open offer. Provided that this regulation shall not prohibit the wilful defaulter from making a competing offer upon any other person making an open offer.
question: Is there a contradiction between Regulation 23(1) and Regulation 6A regarding the circumstances under which a wilful defaulter can withdraw from an open offer obligation?
YOUR_ANSWER: There is NO direct contradiction between Regulation 23(1) and Regulation 6A. They operate at different stages of the open offer process. Regulation 6A is a PRE-OFFER restriction: it prohibits a wilful defaulter from making a public announcement of an open offer in the first instance, or from entering into any transaction that would trigger such an obligation. Regulation 23(1) governs WITHDRAWAL of an open offer that has ALREADY BEEN MADE — it lists the limited grounds (statutory approval refused, death of acquirer, unfulfilled conditions outside the acquirer's control, or Board's opinion) on which an announced open offer can be withdrawn. The exception in Regulation 6A (permitting a wilful defaulter to make a COMPETING offer when another party has already made an open offer) does not conflict with Regulation 23(1), since any such competing offer would itself become subject to the withdrawal restrictions of Regulation 23(1) once made. The two regulations address different phases and are not in contradiction.

Passage B:

question: Do the original Regulation 14(g) and the 2011-amended version impose the same mandatory rating requirement for large debt security issues?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, the original Regulation 14(g) and the 2011-amended version do NOT impose the same mandatory rating requirement. The original Regulation 14(g) imposed a specific, prescriptive obligation: for any issue of debt securities whose size equals or exceeds Rs 100 crore, the client must obtain a rating from AT LEAST TWO DIFFERENT rating agencies — a dual-rating requirement with a quantitative size threshold. The 2011-amended version (substituted w.e.f. 27-12-2011) replaced this with a general obligation: the client must obtain a rating for any issue of debt securities 'in accordance with the relevant regulations' — removing both the specific Rs 100 crore size threshold and the mandatory two-agency requirement. The amended version is a general cross-referencing clause, significantly less prescriptive than the original, and eliminates the dual-rating and threshold requirements entirely.

question: Do the original and 2021-amended versions of Regulation 15(1)(e) cover the same categories of investments requiring 75% investor approval?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, the original and 2021-amended versions of Regulation 15(1)(e) do NOT cover the same categories of investments requiring 75% investor approval. The original (pre-2021) version required 75% investor approval only for AIF investments in its ASSOCIATES. The 2021-amended version (substituted w.e.f. 05-05-2021) expanded the scope to require 75% investor approval for investments in: (a) associates (retained from original), AND (b) units of AIFs managed or sponsored by the Manager, Sponsor, or associates of the Manager or Sponsor (newly added category). The amendment materially widens the restriction by capturing investments in related/affiliated AIFs — a category not covered by the original provision. This reflects a tightening of conflict-of-interest safeguards beyond just associate investments.

context: Regulation 4(g) (original, pre-2020): the key investment team of the Manager of AIF has adequate experience, with at least one key personnel having not less than five years experience in advising or managing pools of capital or in fund or asset or wealth or portfolio management or in the business of buying, selling and dealing of securities or other financial assets and has relevant professional qualification. [Substituted by SEBI (AIF) (Amendment) Regulations, 2020, w.e.f. 19-10-2020]: team has at least one key personnel with relevant NISM certification AND at least one with professional qualification in finance or CFA Charter.
question: How did the SEBI (AIF) (Amendment) Regulations, 2020 change the eligibility requirements for the key investment team of an AIF Manager, and what was the significance of this change?
YOUR_ANSWER: The original Regulation 4(g) (pre-2020) required the key investment team of the AIF Manager to have at least one key personnel with: (i) not less than five years of relevant experience in advising/managing pools of capital, fund/asset/wealth/portfolio management, or buying/selling/dealing in securities or other financial assets, AND (ii) a relevant professional qualification — a combined experience-plus-qualification standard with significant flexibility in what constituted a 'professional qualification.' The SEBI (AIF) (Amendment) Regulations, 2020 (w.e.f. 19-10-2020) substituted this with two distinct, objective requirements: (1) at least one key personnel must hold a relevant NISM certification, AND (2) at least one key personnel must hold a professional qualification in finance or a CFA Charter. Significance: The amendment shifts from an experience-led criterion to formal certification/qualification benchmarks, introducing specific, verifiable standards (NISM certification and finance qualification/CFA Charter) rather than the broader experience test, and the two requirements can be met by the same or different personnel.

context: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996: 'The mutual fund having an aggregate of securities which are worth Rs. 10 crores or more, as on the latest balance-sheet date, shall subject to such instructions as may be issued from time to time by the Board settle their transactions entered on or after January 15, 1998, only through dematerialised securities.' YOUR_ANSWER: Mutual funds with an aggregate of securities worth Rs 10 crore or more (as on the latest balance-sheet date) were required to settle transactions entered on or after JANUARY 15, 1998 only through dematerialised securities. This provision was inserted by the SEBI (Mutual Funds) (Amendment) Regulations, 1998, which came into effect on 12-1-1998, but the mandatory dematerialised settlement obligation applied to transactions entered on or after January 15, 1998.

question: What was the original cap on initial issue expenses for a mutual fund scheme under the Seventh Schedule, and when was this provision omitted?
YOUR_ANSWER: The original Clause 5 of the Seventh Schedule of SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 capped initial issue expenses at SIX PER CENT (6%) of the funds raised under that scheme. [Regulation 8A omitted and Regulation 8(2) substituted by the Change in Conditions of Registration of Certain Intermediaries (Amendment) Regulations, 2016 w.e.f. 08-12-2016.] Current Regulation 8(2): valid unless suspended or cancelled.
question: Describe the evolution of the certificate validity regime for credit rating agencies under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999 from the original regulations through to the current position.
YOUR_ANSWER: The certificate validity regime for CRAs evolved through three distinct phases: Phase 1 (original): Regulation 8(2) provided that the certificate of initial registration was VALID FOR FIVE YEARS. Phase 2 (post-2011 Amendment): Regulation 8A was inserted requiring an application for PERMANENT REGISTRATION to be made three months before the expiry of the initial five-year certificate — creating a two-stage registration structure (initial + permanent). Phase 3 (current, post-2016): Both Regulation 8A and the original Regulation 8(2) were omitted/substituted by the Change in Conditions of Registration of Certain Intermediaries (Amendment) Regulations, 2016 (w.e.f. 08-12-2016). The current Regulation 8(2) provides that the certificate is VALID UNLESS SUSPENDED OR CANCELLED — there is no fixed validity period, and registration continues indefinitely until revoked.

context: Regulation 30 (continual disclosures) was omitted by the SEBI (SAST) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2021, w.e.f. 1-4-2022. Prior to omission, Regulation 30 required every person holding 25%+ and all promoters to disclose their aggregate shareholding as of March 31 each year within 7 working days from year-end. Regulation 29(1) was also substituted by the same amendment, shifting from requiring disclosure only by the acquirer doing the acquisition to requiring disclosure by any acquirer (together with PAC) whose aggregate acquisition reaches 5% or more.
question: What happened to the annual continual disclosure requirement for promoters and major shareholders under SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011, and when was it removed?
YOUR_ANSWER: Regulation 30 (continual disclosures), which required every person holding 25% or more of shares/voting rights and all promoters to disclose their aggregate shareholding as of March 31 each year within 7 working days from year-end, was OMITTED by the SEBI (SAST) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2021, with effect from 1 APRIL 2022. Simultaneously, Regulation 29(1) was substituted by the same amendment, changing the trigger for event-based acquisition disclosure: the original version required disclosure only by the specific acquirer making the acquisition, while the amended version requires disclosure by any acquirer (together with persons acting in concert) whose AGGREGATE acquisition reaches 5% or more — broadening the disclosure obligation.

context: Regulation 5A was substituted by the SEBI (SAST) (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2021, w.e.f. 6-12-2021. The original Regulation 5A (inserted by the SEBI (Listing of Specified Securities on Institutional Trading Platform) Regulations, 2013) read: 'The acquirer may delist the company in accordance with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2009.' The new Regulation 5A provides a detailed delisting offer framework referencing the Delisting Regulations, 2021 and includes a two-attempt structure.
question: How did the SEBI Takeovers Regulations provisions on combined open offer and delisting evolve from 2013 to 2021?
YOUR_ANSWER: The evolution of Regulation 5A proceeded in two stages: Stage 1 (2013): Regulation 5A was INSERTED by the SEBI (Listing of Specified Securities on Institutional Trading Platform) Regulations, 2013 as a single, brief provision simply permitting an acquirer to delist the company in accordance with the SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2009 — a bare cross-reference with no procedural detail. Stage 2 (2021): Regulation 5A was SUBSTITUTED in its entirety by the SEBI (SAST) (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2021 (w.e.f. 6-12-2021), replacing the one-line provision with a detailed delisting offer framework that references the Delisting Regulations, 2021 and includes a TWO-ATTEMPT STRUCTURE for combined open offer and delisting. The change reflects a shift from a bare enabling provision to a comprehensive procedural regime.

context: Regulation 13(e) (as amended w.e.f. 25-11-2025 by SEBI (Investment Advisers) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2025): individuals registered as investment advisers whose number of clients exceed three hundred at any point of time or the fee collected during the financial year exceeds three crore rupees, whichever is earlier shall — (i) immediately intimate the Administration and Supervisory Body and initiate the process of transition from individual to non-individual investment adviser; and (ii) apply for grant of in-principle approval for registration as non-individual investment adviser within 3 months from the date on which the threshold is reached. [Prior to this amendment, per the 2020 version]: individuals... shall — (i) apply for grant of in-principle registration as non-individual investment adviser; (ii) the in-principle registration shall be valid for a period of three months.
question: What procedural change did the SEBI (Investment Advisers) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2025 make to the transition process for individual investment advisers who breach the 300-client or Rs 3 crore fee threshold?
YOUR_ANSWER: The 2020 version of Regulation 13(e) required the individual IA to: (i) apply for grant of in-principle registration as a non-individual investment adviser, with the in-principle registration being valid for a period of three months. It did not explicitly require immediate notification to any supervisory body. The SEBI (Investment Advisers) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2025 (w.e.f. 25-11-2025) changed this to require the individual IA to: (i) IMMEDIATELY INTIMATE the Administration and Supervisory Body AND initiate the process of transition from individual to non-individual IA, AND (ii) apply for grant of in-principle approval for registration as non-individual IA within 3 MONTHS from the date the threshold is reached. The key procedural changes are: (a) addition of an immediate notification obligation to the Administration and Supervisory Body upon breach; (b) an explicit 3-month window for applying for in-principle approval (replacing the in-principle registration being valid for 3 months in the 2020 version); and (c) the framing shifts from obtaining an in-principle 'registration' to applying for 'approval', placing the timeline on the application step.

context: Regulation 10(1)(b)(viii): Invocation of pledge by Scheduled Commercial Banks or Public Financial Institutions as a pledgee was listed as an acquisition in the ordinary course of business exempt from open offer obligations. Regulation 29(4) proviso: the disclosure requirement on encumbrance does not apply to a scheduled commercial bank or public financial institution or a housing finance company or a systemically important non-banking financial company as pledgee. The housing finance company and SBNFC exemption was inserted by the Third Amendment Regulations, 2018, w.e.f. 31-12-2018.
question: When were housing finance companies and systemically important NBFCs added to the list of pledgees exempt from disclosure obligations under the encumbrance provisions of SEBI Takeovers Regulations, and what was the scope of the original exemption?
YOUR_ANSWER: Housing finance companies and systemically important non-banking financial companies (SIBNFCs) were added to the list of pledgees exempt from the encumbrance disclosure obligations under Regulation 29(4) by the SEBI (SAST) THIRD AMENDMENT REGULATIONS, 2018, with effect from 31-12-2018. Original exemption scope: Prior to this 2018 amendment, the proviso to Regulation 29(4) exempted only SCHEDULED COMMERCIAL BANKS and PUBLIC FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS acting as pledgees from the disclosure requirement on encumbrance. The 2018 amendment expanded this to include housing finance companies and SIBNFCs as well.

context: Regulation 22 (original, 2013): Investment advisers which are banks, NBFCs and body corporate providing distribution or execution services to their clients shall keep their investment advisory services segregated from such activities: Provided that such distribution or execution services can only be offered subject to the following: (a) The client shall not be under any obligation to avail the distribution or execution services offered by the investment adviser. (b) The investment adviser shall maintain arms length relationship. (c) All fees and charges paid to distribution or execution service providers by the client shall be paid directly to the service providers and not through the investment adviser. [Substituted by SEBI (IA) (Amendment) Regulations, 2020, w.e.f. 30-09-2020 to require: individual IAs cannot provide distribution services; non-individual IAs to have client-level segregation at group level.]
question: What was the original scope of Regulation 22 in the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013, and how did the 2020 amendment fundamentally change its coverage?
YOUR_ANSWER: Original scope (2013): Regulation 22 applied specifically to BANKS, NBFCs, AND BODY CORPORATES that provided BOTH investment advisory services AND distribution or execution services. It required segregation of advisory from distribution/execution activities, while permitting the dual offering subject to three conditions: (a) client not obligated to use the adviser's distribution/execution services; (b) arm's length relationship maintained; (c) all fees paid directly by client to service providers (not routed through the investment adviser). 2020 Amendment (w.e.f. 30-09-2020): The amendment fundamentally changed coverage in two ways: (1) INDIVIDUAL investment advisers are now PROHIBITED from providing distribution services at all (a categorical ban, not a conditional permission); (2) NON-INDIVIDUAL investment advisers must maintain CLIENT-LEVEL SEGREGATION at the GROUP LEVEL — a stricter structural separation than the earlier arm's length requirement. The amendment thus narrowed the class of permitted dual-service providers and materially tightened the segregation standards.

context: buy-back from the open market through stock exchanges, based on the standalone or consolidated financial statements of the company, whichever sets out a lower amount, shall be less than: (i) fifteen per cent of the paid up capital and free reserves of the company till March 31, 2023; (ii) ten per cent of the paid up capital and free reserves of the company till March 31, 2024; (iii) five per cent of the paid up capital and free reserves of the company till March 31, 2025. Provided further that buy-back from the open market through the stock exchange shall not be allowed with effect from April 1, 2025.
question: Describe the step-by-step reduction in the maximum open-market buy-back limit through stock exchanges under SEBI Regulations, from 2023 to the final prohibition.
YOUR_ANSWER: The open-market buy-back limit through stock exchanges was reduced in three steps before a final prohibition: Step 1: Until 31 March 2023 — maximum limit was LESS THAN 15% of paid-up capital and free reserves (standalone or consolidated, whichever is lower). Step 2: Until 31 March 2024 — maximum limit reduced to LESS THAN 10% of paid-up capital and free reserves. Step 3: Until 31 March 2025 — maximum limit further reduced to LESS THAN 5% of paid-up capital and free reserves. Final prohibition: WITH EFFECT FROM 1 APRIL 2025, buy-back from the open market through the stock exchange is NOT ALLOWED at all — a complete prohibition.
